name: Guidance
notable_features: A different mechanism from every other structured-generation library here. Guidance constrains generation AND allows backtracking over already-generated tokens by re-masking, rather than only restricting the next-token logits. That is why it can do prompt-plus-constraint interleaving in one pass
Constraint system covers any context-free grammar, so long as the backend model has full Guidance support (the README's own qualifier)
Programming-model API: `lm += gen(regex=...)` writes the constraint as part of the program, so constraints are interleaved with generation and with each other

Backend-agnostic by design - README names Transformers, llama.cpp and OpenAI, and the guiding principle is 'if you already have the backend required for your model, you can simply run pip install guidance'

Mock backend for testing: the README highlights local validation of candidate strings and testing full runs with the Mock model, which is the cheapest way to develop a constrained program without a GPU
MIT-licensed, 21787 stars - the largest community of the three structured-generation libraries
Last push 2026-05-21, release 0.3.2 on 2026-03-18, 633 open issues
hardware_caveats: The backtracking mechanism has a real cost the README does not quantify: re-masking and re-running already-generated tokens means recomputation. On a long constrained generation this can be a large multiple of a single forward pass, and the README gives no overhead table - unlike XGrammar, which at least claims near-zero
It is a library, not an engine. scheduling is 'none' and the backend list reflects which host backends Guidance can drive, not backends it implements

Full grammar support requires the backend to have 'full support for Guidance'. Against a plain OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint you get remote generation without the re-masking machinery, so the interesting features degrade

It is NOT the default structured backend in any major serving engine. vLLM's default is XGrammar (see [[niche-xgrammar]]). If you want Guidance's semantics in production you are either in-process or writing your own integration

Its own README comparison, as rendered in [[niche-lm-format-enforcer]]'s table, marks Guidance as lacking batched generation and beam search and not integrating into existing pipelines - both are real limits on using it in a server
Release cadence has slowed: 0.3.2 shipped 2026-03-18 and the last push was 2026-05-21, roughly five months before this record. Still maintained, not urgent
The repo's language breakdown is dominated by Jupyter Notebooks (29MB) over Python (884KB) - it is a research-and-teaching project that happens to be usable in production, and the docs reflect that
best_for: Writing programs that interleave constraints with generation, which no other library in this slice does - regex fields appearing mid-output, conditions on later fields constraining earlier ones
Iterating on a constrained prompt cheaply using the Mock backend, with no GPU
Structured extraction with a grammar you control fully rather than a JSON schema subset
Reading the clearest statement of why re-masking-based steering and logit-restriction-based constraint enforcement are different problems
avoid_for: Production per-token paths in a serving engine - use the engine's default structured backend
Batched generation or beam search, which its peers' comparison tables mark as unsupported
Remote HTTP backends where you need the re-masking features
Latency-critical generation, given the unquantified recomputation cost of backtracking
notes: Fourth of the structured-generation records (with [[niche-xgrammar]], [[niche-outlines]], [[niche-lm-format-enforcer]]) because it is the one with a genuinely different mechanism: it constrains and backtracks rather than only restricting logits. That mechanism is why it survives alongside the logit-restriction libraries rather than being displaced by them. All metadata from the GitHub API on 2026-10-03.
